messages.content:
Work out the ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Think in three steps: first name the condition chiefly responsible for the admission, second name the ICD-10-AM chapter letter it belongs to, third give the three-character category.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: Irreversible airflow limitation in a heavy smoker with an infective exacerbation is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, chapter J, category J44.
CODE: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: ST elevation with a rising troponin and culprit-vessel stenting is an acute myocardial infarction, chapter I, category I21.
CODE: I21

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]

Date of Admission: [REDACTED] - Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]

Hospitalization Reason: Generalized seizure episode, persistent cough, and shortness of breath

Hospital Course:
The patient, a 50-year-old female with a medical history significant for immune thrombocytopenia and seizure disorder was admitted to the ER after experiencing a generalized seizure episode. She reported having a persistent cough, shortness of breath, and recent general malaise.

Upon hospitalization, a chest radiogram revealed bilateral patchy infiltrates, and her oxygen saturation levels were found to be decreasing. She was provided with supplemental oxygen during her stay, and a six-minute walk test was conducted to assess her oxygen levels further. A repeat chest radiogram was done on the third hospital day and revealed significant clearance of the infiltrates with much improvement in her oxygen saturation values both at rest and with ambulation.

Cardiac markers and 2D echocardiogram revealed no notable abnormalities. The patient did not experience any more seizures during hospitalization and remained stable. After four days of observation, the patient was discharged to be followed up in the office.
Diagnoses: [diagnosis section withheld]
Follow Up:
The patient was discharged to be followed up in the office, where her symptoms and overall health will be evaluated by a medical professional regularly. 

Conclusion:
The patient was admitted to the hospital on [REDACTED] after experiencing a generalized seizure episode and other symptoms. After four days of observation and treatment, the patient's condition improved, and she was discharged with instructions to follow up in the office. She was diagnosed with non-cardiogenic pulmonary edema based on her presenting symptoms.

Write your reasoning in at most three short sentences, then a final line of exactly 'CODE: <letter><digit><digit>'.

text:
The condition chiefly responsible for the stay was non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, likely neurogenic after the seizure; it caused the infiltrates and falling oxygen saturation, and was the focus of oxygen therapy and monitoring. The seizure disorder could be argued as principal, but she had no further seizures and the discharge diagnosis names the oedema. Pulmonary oedema sits in chapter J, category J81.

CODE: J81
